opus-5.5.text:
I think the most exciting part is that we've only scratched the surface. With s1, the core finding was surprisingly simple: take a strong base model, fine-tune it on just about a thousand carefully chosen reasoning examples, and then use what we call budget forcing to control how long it thinks. If it tries to stop too early, you append something like "Wait," and the model often reconsiders and fixes its own mistakes. That alone gave us a nice scaling curve, where more test-time compute led to better performance on things like competition math.

But that curve eventually flattens. With budget forcing, if you keep suppressing the end of thinking, at some point the model starts repeating itself or going in circles, partly because you hit the context window. So one big direction is figuring out how to keep scaling without that plateau. Can you combine sequential scaling, where the model thinks longer in a single chain, with parallel approaches like sampling many chains and aggregating them? Can the model learn to summarize or compress its own reasoning so it isn't bounded by context length? I think there's a lot of headroom there.

The second thing I'm excited about is going beyond math and science benchmarks. Those were convenient because you can verify answers, but the same idea of letting a model spend more compute when a problem is hard should apply to coding, to agentic tasks where the model interacts with an environment over many steps, and to open-ended research-style problems. Extending test-time scaling to settings where the model is acting rather than only reasoning is where it becomes really useful.

And finally, there's the efficiency and openness angle. Part of the point of s1 was to show you don't need a huge, secret recipe to get this behavior. A small, high-quality dataset and a simple intervention go a long way. So I'm excited about the community building on that: better data selection, better ways to decide how much compute a given question deserves, and making these reasoning capabilities accessible with fully open models, data, and code. If we can make models that know when to think hard and when to answer quickly, that's a big step toward systems that are both more capable and more practical.

r001.rationale: It says suppressing the end of thinking eventually makes the model repeat itself or go in circles, and that the scaling curve flattens.

r002.rationale: It identifies the context window as a reason the model cannot keep extending sequential reasoning.

r003.rationale: It mentions sampling many chains and aggregating them, but does not explain that this lets test-time computation exceed the token limit of a single generation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the most exciting thing for me is actually how simple it turned out to be. With s1 we took a thousand carefully curated examples, did supervised fine-tuning on Qwen2.5-32B, and then just controlled how long the model thinks at test time with this budget forcing trick, where you literally append the word "Wait" when the model tries to stop, and that gets it to keep reasoning and often correct itself. And that alone gets you a curve where more test-time compute reliably gives you better performance on things like AIME and MATH. So the first exciting direction is just: how far does that curve go? Right now it flattens out at some point, partly because of context length and partly because the model starts to loop. So one thing I'm interested in is whether you can combine budget forcing with something like parallel sampling or tree-style search so that the extrapolation doesn't saturate as early.

The second thing, and I think this is maybe underexplored, is that we showed you don't need a huge amount of data to unlock this behavior. The capability was already in the base model from pretraining, and the thousand samples are more about teaching it the format and getting it to actually use the reasoning. That makes me think the real lever is still in pretraining, so I'm excited about what happens when you design the pretraining data with this in mind, rather than treating test-time scaling as a purely post-training phenomenon.

And then the third piece is going beyond math and code. Those domains are nice because you can verify answers, but a lot of what people actually want is open-ended, like writing or research or agentic tasks where there isn't a single correct answer. So the question is how you do test-time scaling, and how you even measure it, when the reward isn't clean. I think if you can make "think longer and you get better" work for those kinds of tasks, that's when it becomes really transformative, and that's honestly the thing I'm most curious about right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the performance curve flattens partly because the model starts to loop after budget forcing extends its reasoning.

r002.rationale: It names context length as a cause of flattening, but does not explain that a fixed context window limits how long the model can continue sequential reasoning.

r003.rationale: It mentions parallel sampling as a way to delay saturation, but does not explain aggregating parallel generations to scale computation beyond an individual generation’s token limit.

astra-6.text:
What I find most exciting is giving models more flexibility in how much they think. Some questions need a quick answer; others might benefit from much more computation. With s1, we explored a simple way of extending that thinking at test time. The next question is whether we can make that process more adaptive: can the model figure out when more thinking is useful, when to try a different approach, and when to stop?

Just producing a longer chain of thought isn’t necessarily enough. You want that additional computation to go toward checking an assumption, catching a mistake, or exploring an alternative solution. If we can get that right, then test-time compute becomes a really useful way to improve a model’s capabilities without having to retrain it for every harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention repetitive looping or say that repeatedly prompting s1 to “wait” eventually stops improving answers.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify a fixed context window as a limit on sequential reasoning.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe aggregating parallel generations to scale computation beyond one generation’s token limit.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find most exciting is the idea that a model can decide how much to think based on the problem. For a simple question, you want a quick answer. For a really difficult math or coding problem, you might be happy to wait longer if that extra computation gives you a better result.

With s1, we explored a very simple way to control that: when the model tries to stop thinking, we can append “Wait” and let it continue. Sometimes it checks its work, finds a mistake, and corrects it. But extending the reasoning doesn’t always help, so there’s a lot to understand about how to use that additional compute productively.

That’s the direction I’m excited about: moving from simply making the model think longer to having it recognize when more thinking is useful, what to spend that thinking on, and when to stop.
